metadata.narrative: Write a technical proposal for a distributed audio streaming system. The system should include an audio streaming platform and a live chat feature. This application should be built for both browser and mobile settings. Include detailed technologies and justify why they are used. Assume the audience is a team of experienced software developers at a medium sized software company.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: This proposal describes a distributed system that delivers an audio streaming platform with an integrated live chat feature to both browser and native mobile clients for an experienced engineering team.

The design follows a microservices architecture in which independently scalable services communicate through synchronous APIs and asynchronous event streams, letting the streaming and chat subsystems scale and fail independently of one another.

Broadcasters push audio into the platform using the WebRTC-HTTP Ingestion Protocol, which signals a WebRTC session over HTTP while preserving WebRTC's end-to-end encryption and sub-second latency, with RTMP supported as a fallback ingest path for legacy hardware encoders that have not adopted WHIP.
RTMP remains useful for first-mile delivery because its persistent TCP handshake-connection-stream model is mature and broadly supported, even though it trades some latency for that compatibility.

A transcoding service then produces multiple renditions through transrating and transmuxing so a single incoming stream can be adaptively delivered at bitrates matching each listener's bandwidth, the mechanism behind adaptive bitrate streaming.

We encode with Opus for interactive, low-latency paths and AAC for stored or broadcast-compatible renditions, since Opus is purpose-built for low algorithmic delay and outperforms AMR-WB, AAC, and Vorbis across a wide bitrate range, while AAC offers broader device and platform compatibility.

For playback we support Low-Latency HLS and WebRTC side by side: LL-HLS gives adaptive-bitrate quality and wide CDN and device compatibility at 2-8 second latency over TCP, while WebRTC's UDP transport and push-based RTP delivery reach sub-second latency for interactive listening.

Renditions are distributed through a CDN, which places content physically closer to listeners, reduces buffering, mitigates DDoS exposure, and improves perceived quality by shortening the network path.

The live chat feature follows the seven-component pattern common to production chat systems: application server, load balancer, streaming event manager, authentication/user manager, presence, media store, and database.

Client-server delivery uses WebSocket for guaranteed in-order TCP delivery, since WebRTC's UDP transport offers no ordering guarantees and would force us to reimplement retry and ordering logic ourselves.

Because WebSocket connections are stateful, horizontal scaling requires either a managed API Gateway that stores connection identifiers in a fast key-value store and fans messages out through a queue-triggered function, or a self-hosted fleet fronted by a pub/sub layer, since one instance otherwise cannot know which users are connected elsewhere.

We use Apache Kafka as the event-streaming backbone between chat, presence, and notification services because its partitioned, replicated publish-subscribe log gives the throughput and durability chat traffic needs, while simpler point-to-point queues handle isolated background jobs; Kafka clusters are secured with SSL authentication, per-topic access-control lists, and encryption in transit.

For chat history we favor a column-family store modeled on Cassandra's partition/clustering key design, following the pattern large chat systems adopt once single-node indexes and random reads become unpredictable at scale; a composite key such as (channel_id, bucket, message_id) keeps related messages contiguous and lets nodes be added linearly as history grows.

DynamoDB is an acceptable managed alternative for teams already on AWS wanting seamless scaling without operating a cluster, while Cassandra suits teams wanting direct control over multi-datacenter replication; both support encryption at rest and in transit.

Redis sits alongside these stores as an in-memory cache and pub/sub layer for presence, recent-chat caching, session storage, and streaming metadata such as CDN manifest and auth-token caching, trading unlimited capacity for very low latency.
Increasing the number of concurrent connections handled per host, as achieved industry-wide through Erlang and FreeBSD kernel tuning, reduces the chat tier's server footprint and cost.

On the client side, browsers get native WebRTC support with hardware-accelerated codecs plus Media Source Extensions for HLS-style playback, Android clients use Google's ExoPlayer for DASH, HLS, SmoothStreaming, and Widevine-protected playback, and iOS clients use Apple's AVPlayer, which natively supports HTTPS Live Streaming and a wide range of audio containers.

For the mobile chat and shell UI we recommend a cross-platform framework, React Native or Flutter, so the team ships one codebase to iOS and Android; React Native suits teams already fluent in JavaScript/TypeScript reusing existing React logic, while Flutter's ahead-of-time compiled Dart delivers more consistent native-like performance and a single reusable widget set.

Authentication spans both subsystems through a shared API Gateway that terminates OAuth2/OpenID Connect flows and issues JSON Web Tokens, exchanging an external token for an internal service token before forwarding requests downstream.

Service-to-service calls use a distinct service identity, via API keys or client-credential access tokens, separate from end-user identity, letting us audit user actions and rate-limit machine callers independently.
Baseline practice requires encrypting all communications, never hard-coding secrets, multi-factor administrative authentication, and container-level controls layered beneath gateway enforcement.

Deployment runs on Kubernetes, which automates provisioning, self-healing, rolling updates, and horizontal autoscaling of each microservice's containers, giving the streaming pipeline and chat tier independent scaling policies during traffic spikes such as a popular live show.

Beyond the scheduler itself, the team should standardize CI/CD, deployment strategy such as blue-green or canary releases, and ownership of the orchestration foundation, since running Kubernetes alone does not solve configuration, security, or observability concerns.

Observability combines structured logs, time-series metrics, and distributed traces, collected with OpenTelemetry instrumentation and exported to Prometheus for metrics and Jaeger for request tracing across the microservice graph.

Prometheus's pull-based scraping and label-rich time series pair naturally with Kubernetes' dynamic service discovery, letting Grafana dashboards and alerts adapt automatically as chat and streaming services scale up or down.

Together, WHIP/RTMP ingest, Opus/AAC transcoding, LL-HLS/WebRTC delivery through a CDN, a Kafka- and WebSocket-driven chat tier backed by Cassandra or DynamoDB and Redis, OAuth2/JWT security at a shared gateway, and Kubernetes-orchestrated deployment with full-stack observability give a medium-sized team a technology stack that is well-documented, independently scalable per subsystem, and consistent across browser and mobile clients.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

k.description: Number of fused passages to return (default 10).

documents.description: Evidence-worthy staged documents to retain. An empty array explicitly rejects the whole staged batch.

answer.text: This proposal describes a distributed system that delivers an audio streaming platform with an integrated live chat feature to both browser and native mobile clients for an experienced engineering team.

The design follows a microservices architecture in which independently scalable services communicate through synchronous APIs and asynchronous event streams, letting the streaming and chat subsystems scale and fail independently of one another.

Broadcasters push audio into the platform using the WebRTC-HTTP Ingestion Protocol, which signals a WebRTC session over HTTP while preserving WebRTC's end-to-end encryption and sub-second latency, with RTMP supported as a fallback ingest path for legacy hardware encoders that have not adopted WHIP.
RTMP remains useful for first-mile delivery because its persistent TCP handshake-connection-stream model is mature and broadly supported, even though it trades some latency for that compatibility.

A transcoding service then produces multiple renditions through transrating and transmuxing so a single incoming stream can be adaptively delivered at bitrates matching each listener's bandwidth, the mechanism behind adaptive bitrate streaming.

We encode with Opus for interactive, low-latency paths and AAC for stored or broadcast-compatible renditions, since Opus is purpose-built for low algorithmic delay and outperforms AMR-WB, AAC, and Vorbis across a wide bitrate range, while AAC offers broader device and platform compatibility.

For playback we support Low-Latency HLS and WebRTC side by side: LL-HLS gives adaptive-bitrate quality and wide CDN and device compatibility at 2-8 second latency over TCP, while WebRTC's UDP transport and push-based RTP delivery reach sub-second latency for interactive listening.

Renditions are distributed through a CDN, which places content physically closer to listeners, reduces buffering, mitigates DDoS exposure, and improves perceived quality by shortening the network path.

The live chat feature follows the seven-component pattern common to production chat systems: application server, load balancer, streaming event manager, authentication/user manager, presence, media store, and database.

Client-server delivery uses WebSocket for guaranteed in-order TCP delivery, since WebRTC's UDP transport offers no ordering guarantees and would force us to reimplement retry and ordering logic ourselves.

Because WebSocket connections are stateful, horizontal scaling requires either a managed API Gateway that stores connection identifiers in a fast key-value store and fans messages out through a queue-triggered function, or a self-hosted fleet fronted by a pub/sub layer, since one instance otherwise cannot know which users are connected elsewhere.

We use Apache Kafka as the event-streaming backbone between chat, presence, and notification services because its partitioned, replicated publish-subscribe log gives the throughput and durability chat traffic needs, while simpler point-to-point queues handle isolated background jobs; Kafka clusters are secured with SSL authentication, per-topic access-control lists, and encryption in transit.

For chat history we favor a column-family store modeled on Cassandra's partition/clustering key design, following the pattern large chat systems adopt once single-node indexes and random reads become unpredictable at scale; a composite key such as (channel_id, bucket, message_id) keeps related messages contiguous and lets nodes be added linearly as history grows.

DynamoDB is an acceptable managed alternative for teams already on AWS wanting seamless scaling without operating a cluster, while Cassandra suits teams wanting direct control over multi-datacenter replication; both support encryption at rest and in transit.

Redis sits alongside these stores as an in-memory cache and pub/sub layer for presence, recent-chat caching, session storage, and streaming metadata such as CDN manifest and auth-token caching, trading unlimited capacity for very low latency.
Increasing the number of concurrent connections handled per host, as achieved industry-wide through Erlang and FreeBSD kernel tuning, reduces the chat tier's server footprint and cost.

On the client side, browsers get native WebRTC support with hardware-accelerated codecs plus Media Source Extensions for HLS-style playback, Android clients use Google's ExoPlayer for DASH, HLS, SmoothStreaming, and Widevine-protected playback, and iOS clients use Apple's AVPlayer, which natively supports HTTPS Live Streaming and a wide range of audio containers.

For the mobile chat and shell UI we recommend a cross-platform framework, React Native or Flutter, so the team ships one codebase to iOS and Android; React Native suits teams already fluent in JavaScript/TypeScript reusing existing React logic, while Flutter's ahead-of-time compiled Dart delivers more consistent native-like performance and a single reusable widget set.

Authentication spans both subsystems through a shared API Gateway that terminates OAuth2/OpenID Connect flows and issues JSON Web Tokens, exchanging an external token for an internal service token before forwarding requests downstream.

Service-to-service calls use a distinct service identity, via API keys or client-credential access tokens, separate from end-user identity, letting us audit user actions and rate-limit machine callers independently.
Baseline practice requires encrypting all communications, never hard-coding secrets, multi-factor administrative authentication, and container-level controls layered beneath gateway enforcement.

Deployment runs on Kubernetes, which automates provisioning, self-healing, rolling updates, and horizontal autoscaling of each microservice's containers, giving the streaming pipeline and chat tier independent scaling policies during traffic spikes such as a popular live show.

Beyond the scheduler itself, the team should standardize CI/CD, deployment strategy such as blue-green or canary releases, and ownership of the orchestration foundation, since running Kubernetes alone does not solve configuration, security, or observability concerns.

Observability combines structured logs, time-series metrics, and distributed traces, collected with OpenTelemetry instrumentation and exported to Prometheus for metrics and Jaeger for request tracing across the microservice graph.

Prometheus's pull-based scraping and label-rich time series pair naturally with Kubernetes' dynamic service discovery, letting Grafana dashboards and alerts adapt automatically as chat and streaming services scale up or down.

Together, WHIP/RTMP ingest, Opus/AAC transcoding, LL-HLS/WebRTC delivery through a CDN, a Kafka- and WebSocket-driven chat tier backed by Cassandra or DynamoDB and Redis, OAuth2/JWT security at a shared gateway, and Kubernetes-orchestrated deployment with full-stack observability give a medium-sized team a technology stack that is well-documented, independently scalable per subsystem, and consistent across browser and mobile clients.
